Hanun
HAY-nun
proper noun
Hebrew Chanun, “favoured” or “gracious,” the Ammonite king who insulted David’s messengers.

See also: Hanun

Biblical Definition

Hanun was the son of Nahash and king of the Ammonites after him, who repaid David’s kindness with a grievous insult that brought war upon his people. When Nahash died, David sought to show kindness to Hanun for his father’s sake, and sent his servants to comfort him (2Sa 10:2). But the princes of Ammon persuaded Hanun that the messengers were spies; so Hanun took David’s servants, shaved off the one half of their beards, and cut off their garments in the middle, even to their hinder parts, and sent them away in shame (2Sa 10:4). This deliberate disgrace of an embassy of peace was an act of war, and the Ammonites, knowing they had made themselves odious to David, hired the Syrians to fight for them. But the LORD gave Israel the victory over both Ammon and Syria (2Sa 10:6–19). Hanun, whose name means “gracious,” acted with the opposite of grace, turning kindness into an occasion of contempt. He stands as a warning against the folly of repaying goodwill with insult, and the listening to evil counsel that turns a friend into an enemy. His insolence brought ruin upon his own house and people.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Ammonite king, son of Nahash, who insulted David’s messengers and brought war upon his people.

expand to see more

HANUN, the son of Nahash, king of the Ammonites.

David sought to show him kindness for his father’s sake (2Sa 10:2).

Persuaded the messengers were spies, he shamed them (2Sa 10:4).

He shaved their beards and cut off their garments in disgrace.

His insult brought war, in which Israel overcame Ammon and Syria (2Sa 10:6–19).

Key Scripture

2Sa 10:2 — "Then said David, I will shew kindness unto Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father shewed kindness unto me. And David sent to comfort him by the hand of his servants for his father. And David's servants came into the land of the children of Ammon."

2Sa 10:4 — "Wherefore Hanun took David's servants, and shaved off the one half of their beards, and cut off their garments in the middle, even to their buttocks, and sent them away."

2Sa 10:6 — "And when the children of Ammon saw that they stank before David, the children of Ammon sent and hired the Syrians of Bethrehob, and the Syrians of Zoba, twenty thousand footmen, and of king Maacah a thousand men, and of Ishtob twelve thousand men."

1Ch 19:5 — "Then there went certain, and told David how the men were served. And he sent to meet them: for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, Tarry at Jericho until your beards be grown, and then return."

Modern Corruption

A figure of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; he warns against repaying kindness with insult and heeding evil counsel.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the folly of repaying goodwill with contempt. David sent kindness, and Hanun, listening to suspicious counsellors, returned a deliberate insult that turned a friend into an enemy and brought war upon his land. He that returns evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house (Prov 17:13). The bitter fruit of Hanun’s insolence was the ruin of his people.

Hanun’s heeding of evil counsel is a further warning. His princes filled his ears with suspicion against an embassy of peace, and he believed them to his destruction. Whom a man listens to shapes what he becomes; the counsel of the malicious leads to ruin. His name, “gracious,” stands in sharp rebuke over his graceless act, a reminder that a fair name is no guarantee of a fair heart.

Hebrew Roots

The name means “favoured” or “gracious,” standing in irony over his graceless deed.

expand to see more

Hanun — Hebrew Chanun, “favoured” or “gracious.”

The root chanan means to be gracious or to show favour.

He was the son of Nahash, king of the Ammonites.

He insulted David’s messengers of peace.

His name stands in irony over his graceless act.

Usage

"Like Hanun, those who repay kindness with insult bring evil upon their own house."

"Hanun teaches that heeding malicious counsel turns a friend into an enemy and leads to ruin."

"His gracious name over a graceless deed warns that a fair name is no guarantee of a fair heart."
